title: Did Climate Cause the Collapse of the Maya?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether climate change caused the collapse of the Classic Maya civilization between roughly 800 and 950 CE. They open with Charles Lindbergh's 1929 flight over the Central American jungle and the rediscovery of lost Maya cities, then cover the Classic period's prosperity, the collapse, and theories including overfarming, warfare, disease, and drought. Cave-deposit and lake-sediment evidence points to a wet period followed by a long drought around 660 CE, and deforestation may have worsened local warming and drought. The hosts extend the idea to the Neo-Assyrian Empire, Angkor/Khmer Empire, Norse Greenland, and the Syrian civil war, then discuss population growth, modern agriculture, and long-term thinking. The episode closes with a listener mail from Rosanna in Surrey, UK.

segments.title: Opening banter and live show plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote January live shows in Seattle and San Francisco, then open with joking banter about the topic and how to order the episode.

segments.title: Charles Lindbergh and the rediscovered Maya cities
segments.summary: Lindbergh, flying for Pan Am over Central America, spots a stone temple with twin reflecting pools; the hosts note the popular story that he discovered the lost Maya is apocryphal, though lost cities were being found from the 1920s onward, many with large pyramids.

segments.title: The Classic Maya period and its prosperity
segments.summary: The Classic period (roughly 250 to 900 CE) saw cities of 60,000 to 70,000 people, pyramids, calendars, and math. The Maya were divided into warring city-states, and between about 800 and 950 CE the classic culture largely vanished, though people assimilated into other cultures.

segments.title: Lidar, hieroglyphs, and the Maya legend
segments.summary: The hosts discuss lidar revealing hidden structures under jungle, including El Mirador, and the decipherment of Maya hieroglyphs, recommended via a Nova documentary.

segments.title: Competing theories: overfarming, warfare, disease
segments.summary: Explanations for the collapse include overfarming from population growth, warfare that drained resources and provoked retaliation, and disease from a crop virus. The hosts note these are not mutually exclusive.

segments.title: Climate records: wet period then drought
segments.summary: Cave deposit (speleothem) records show a wet period that supported Maya growth, followed by the longest dry spell in two thousand years around 660 CE. The Petén region depended on reservoirs, so drought threatened thirst, unrest, and conflict.

segments.title: Deforestation and local warming
segments.summary: Pollen records in lake sediment show a shift from tree to weed pollen around 800 CE, as Maya cleared forests for slash-and-burn farming. A NASA model estimated local temperature rose about six degrees Fahrenheit, which could worsen drought.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a brief banter tangent.

segments.title: Climate and other civilizations: Assyria, Khmer, Vikings
segments.summary: The hosts describe a broader view of collapses: a wet-then-dry record at Kuna Ba cave in northern Iraq matching the Neo-Assyrian Empire, a drought linked to the Khmer Empire and Angkor Wat, and the Norse abandonment of Greenland during the Little Ice Age.

segments.title: Modern parallels: Syria, deforestation, population
segments.summary: The hosts connect the pattern to modern times: a drought from 2006 may have driven farmers into Syrian cities, contributing to the Syrian civil war. They discuss tree loss in North America, projected population of ten billion, the Green Revolution, and fertilizer runoff.

segments.title: Long-term thinking and skepticism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why people fail to plan for future generations, the idea of longer lifespans, and skepticism that climate-driven collapse is a trendy or unproven framing, while noting farming may need to become more sustainable.

segments.title: Listener mail from Rosanna in Surrey
segments.summary: Rosanna writes that she and her husband are renovating an Edwardian house and that the show keeps her company during long solo work days. Josh and Chuck respond and give the mail address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and information on contacting the show.
